single.question: Do barnacles have a free-swimming larval stage?

memories.memory: in my own opinion, the Limulus-like larva in 1st stage;—the mouthless pupa;—especially the method of cement with its modifications;—the senses;—& homologies & sexual peculiarities,—are the most curious points

single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply: I have not heard of a larval stage in the barnacles; but I have seen the young ones in the mud, and I am very much surprised to find them so small and delicate.

single.question: What do you make of Hooker's view of the Tasmanian flora?
single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply: I have not heard Hooker’s views upon the subject. I am very glad to hear that he has found the Australian Flora very much like the Tasmanian Flora. It is a matter of some interest to me. I have read Hooker’s works several times, and I have never heard him say so.

single.question: Did the Beagle voyage change your mind about species?

memories.memory: I have been attending a very little to species of birds, & the passages of forms, do appear frightful—every thing is arbitrary; no two naturalists agree on any fundamental idea that I can see

single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply: I have not been much interested in the Beagle voyage. I was very much interested in the Geology, & in the Flora, & I found that the Geology & Flora were both inextricably entangled with the Zoology. I have not much to say about the Zoology, but I was quite as much interested in it, as in the Geology & Flora.

single.question: Can seeds survive immersion in sea-water?

memories.memory: The seed of Capsicum, after 137 days’ immersion, came up well, for 30 out of 56 planted germinated, and I think more would have grown with time

I have begun making some few experiments on the effects of immersion in sea-water on the germinating powers of seeds, in the hope of being able to throw a very little light on the distribution of plants

As out of these 23 kinds of seed, selected almost at hap-hazard, the five Leguminosæ alone have as yet been killed (with the exception of the Cabbage seed, and these have survived in the ice-cold water), one is tempted to infer that the seeds of this family must generally withstand salt water much worse than the seeds of the other great natural families; yet from remarks in botanical works, I had expected that these would have survived longest

I have begun my seed-salting experiments, & I shd. be extremely much obliged if you would tell me what kinds you would expect to be most easily killed by sea-water besides the Cruciferæ, which I had thought wd. be so, & which you confirmed
The cress & Lettuce has just vegetated well after 21 days immersion

single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply:
I have been thinking much of your question, & am glad to say that I have tried it, & found that the Cress, & Lettuce & Bean, survived immersion in sea-water better than the seeds of any other plant

I have tried a great many seeds, & found that the Leguminosæ generally, survived better than other seeds, but the Cress, Lettuce & Bean were the best survivors

single.question: What caused the First World War?
single.thinking: Nothing I have written before bears on this directly.
single.reply: I have not been able to make any progress in the subject of the causes of the war, but I have been led to the conclusion, that it was due to the combination of two events: (1) the rise of Germany, which I think is a case of a new nation becoming a power; and (2) the fact that the alliance of France, Germany and Austria was broken up by the action of the two latter powers in the Balkan Peninsula, which had been the object of the alliance.
